extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of political economy/public policy
extracted.subtask_short: analysis of laissez-faire and state intervention
extracted.subtask_description: A historical and analytical discussion of the doctrine of laissez-faire, the causes that expand government action, classifications of forms of legislative intervention, and criteria for assessing the effects of such legislation in the United States and comparative contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentimental foundation of Laissez faire
rubrics_metrics.description: The sentimental ground is the desire of the individual to be let alone, to do as he pleases, indulge his impulses, follow out his projects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This foundation emphasizes personal liberty and the individual's wish not to be interfered with by government; it is rooted in national character and constitutional proclamations of individual liberty (e.g., Declaration of Independence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rational foundation of Laissez faire
rubrics_metrics.description: The rational ground is the principle, gathered from an observation of the phenomena of society, that interference by government more often does harm than good — that is to say, that the desires and impulses of men when left to themselves are more likely by their natural collision and co-operation to work out a happy result for the community and the individuals than will be attained by the conscious endeavours of the State controlling and directing those desires and impulses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument based on experience/observation and belief in social 'laws of nature' governing mankind; holds that individuals thrive better under these natural laws than under rules made by government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes tending to lengthen the arms of government
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern civilization, in becoming more complex and refined, discerns more benefits which the organized power of government can secure; men live fast and are impatient of the slow working of natural laws; triumphs of physical science have enlarged desires for comfort and shown what collective skill and large funds can accomplish; there is a quickened moral sensitiveness and philanthropic sympathy; freedom of association has enabled groups and corporations to overshadow individuals; transference of political power from the few to the many makes the many less jealous of governmental authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These factors are offered as reasons why governments expand their activities both in Europe and the United States; the passage discusses how each cause operates to increase demand for state action and how democratic control can make the populace turn readily to government for solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibitions to individuals to do acts which are not, in the ordinary sense of the word, criminal
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibitions to individuals to do acts which are not, in the ordinary sense of the word, criminal (e.g. to sell intoxicating liquors, to employ a labourer for more than so many hours in a day).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is one of the principal forms of legislative intervention; examples and many state statutes illustrate how moral or social concerns are criminalized or prohibited even though the acts might not traditionally be considered crimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directions to individuals to do things which it is not obviously wrong to omit
rubrics_metrics.description: Directions to individuals to do things which it is not obviously wrong to omit (e.g. to provide seats for shop-women, to publish the accounts of a railway company).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislation may require affirmative actions by private persons or firms for social or administrative objectives; these are distinct from prohibitions and aim at achieving public goods or transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interferences with the ordinary course of law to protect individuals from consequences of their own acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Interferences with the ordinary course of law in order to protect individuals from the consequences of their own acts (e.g. the annulment of contracts between employer and workmen making the former not liable for accidental injuries to the latter, the exemption of homesteads or of a certain amount of personal property from the claims of creditors, the prohibition of more than a certain rate of interest on money).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutes or constitutional provisions may alter private-law outcomes to shield vulnerable parties (workmen, debtors) or limit contractual freedom for perceived social justice or protective purposes; many U.S. examples are cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directions to a public authority to undertake work which might be left to individual action
rubrics_metrics.description: Directions to a public authority to undertake work which might be left to individual action and the operation of supply and demand (e.g. the providing of schools and dispensaries, the establishment of State analysts, State oil inspectors, the collection and diffusion, at the public expense, of statistics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Government is directed to provide services or infrastructure where collective provision is thought more effective; the text lists education, public health, inspection, and statistical services as examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retention, appropriation, or control by the State of certain natural sources of wealth or elements in its production
rubrics_metrics.description: Retention, appropriation, or control by the State of certain natural sources of wealth or elements in its production (e.g. declarations that the use of all waters within the state's bounds is a public use and forever subject to State control; prohibitions of wasteful use of natural gas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States may assert control over natural resources or aspects of production to regulate use, prevent waste, or secure public benefit; examples from western U.S. states are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation criteria for the results of state legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions to ask: What has been the result of this legislation? Have the effects which the economists of the physiocratic or laissez-faire school taught us to expect actually followed? Has the natural course of commerce and industry been disturbed, has the self-helpfulness of the citizen been weakened, has government done its work ill and a new door to jobbery been opened?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage presents these as the standard consequences critics of intervention predict; it also notes that it is too soon to form definitive conclusions, that some experiments have failed and others succeeded, and that U.S. legislatures provide useful data for testing policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character of American state intervention (helps majority, restrains few)
rubrics_metrics.description: State intervention has usually taken the form of helping or protecting the greater number, while restraining the few; personal freedom was at first infringed only at the bidding of a strong moral sentiment (e.g., that which condemns intemperance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This observation explains why Americans accepted particular paternalistic measures more readily: interventions were framed as benefiting the majority or addressing strong moral concerns, which made gradual expansion of state functions less contested.
